title: Chapter 2: LLMs, Prompts, Tokens and a Reusable API Client
content:
Chapter 2: LLMs, Prompts, Tokens and a Reusable API Client

Giving the Model Call Its Own Place

The Chapter 1 assistant takes a code snippet, sends a prompt to a language model and displays an explanation. The API call sits inside that project’s main implementation. As you build more applications, copying that setup would leave you with several versions to maintain.

In this chapter, you will move the provider-specific work into a class called LLMClient. The rest of an application will call it through one method:

response = client.complete(
    system="You are a helpful assistant.",
    user="Explain Python lists.",
)

This separates the request an application wants to make from the details of sending it. We will also examine the concepts behind the call: LLMs, prompts, tokens, context, APIs, models, temperature, cost and latency. Understanding those terms will help you decide what to send, how to configure the request and which parts to test without a live model.

What You Will Learn

  • What a language model does within a Python application.
  • How prompts, system instructions and user requests shape the input.
  • How tokens and context length affect the amount of information in a request.
  • How model choice and settings relate to quality, speed and cost.
  • How to configure an API client without hardcoding secrets.
  • How to write a reusable client, test with a mock and keep provider-specific code separate.

Problems the Client Helps You Manage

Repeated API setup is difficult to maintain: a change to a model setting or request format may require edits in several files. Prompts scattered through unrelated functions create a similar problem. Keeping the API client, prompt templates, application logic and tests separate makes each easier to inspect.

You also need to account for missing keys, incorrect model names, long inputs, network failures, unclear prompts and unnecessary or expensive calls. The client developed here handles a small part of that work, including configuration and empty-input checks. It also provides a place to add further handling as your applications grow.

2.1 What Is an LLM?

LLM stands for Large Language Model. For the text applications in this book, you provide text input and receive generated text. For example, you might send:

Explain what a Python dictionary is.

An illustrative response is:

A Python dictionary stores data as key-value pairs.

A language model can help explain, summarise, rewrite, classify, answer questions, assist with code, plan and draft. It can also reason over context supplied with a request. The usefulness of the result depends on the task, the information provided and how you check the response.

Your Python application remains responsible for receiving user input, reading files, handling API keys, building prompts and displaying results. Tools, memory, retrieval, validation, error handling and deployment also belong to the application design. The model supplies a capability within that larger system.

2.2 What Is a Prompt?

A prompt tells the model what you want it to do. A short request may be enough for an open-ended answer:

Explain Python lists.

If you have a particular reader in mind, specify the audience and the kind of explanation:

Explain Python lists for a beginner.

Use one short example.

Avoid advanced jargon.

You can also define the response structure:

You are a friendly Python tutor.

Explain Python lists for a beginner.

Return:

  1. Short definition
  2. Simple example
  3. Common mistake
  4. Beginner-friendly summary

The third version gives a role, audience, task, format and constraints. Those details make your expectations explicit. They also give you a basis for evaluating the answer: did it explain the concept at the right level, include an example and follow the requested sections?

2.3 System Instructions and User Requests

Separating stable instructions from the current request makes prompts easier to maintain. The stable instructions describe the assistant’s expected behaviour; the user request describes the task for this call.

System Instruction

For a tutoring assistant, the instruction might be:

You are a helpful Python tutor.

Be clear, accurate, and beginner-friendly.

Do not invent facts.

User Request

The user can then ask a specific question:

Explain the difference between a list and a tuple.

The combined input contains both parts:

System:

You are a helpful Python tutor.

User:

Explain the difference between a list and a tuple.

You can reuse the tutor instructions while changing the question. The repaired client sends the stable text in the Responses API’s instructions field and the user request in input. Its build_input() method still returns labelled text for local inspection, but that combined string is not sent as the live request.

2.4 What Are Tokens?

A token is a piece of text that a model processes. Depending on how the text is divided, it may represent a word, part of a word, punctuation, whitespace or a symbol. More text generally means more tokens, although character and word counts are only rough guides.

Token usage matters when considering cost, response time and how much information fits into a request. A RAG application that sends 20 pages of context on every call will usually send more tokens than one that retrieves only the relevant passages. That makes chunking, retrieval and prompt design part of managing the request, as well as part of obtaining a useful answer.

2.5 What Is Context Length?

Context length concerns the amount of information a model can work with in a request. Your input can include system instructions, the user message, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool results and other prompt text. These all contribute to the material the model has to consider.

Sending too much can exceed limits or increase cost. Even if it fits, unrelated material can make the intended task harder to isolate. Choose context because it helps answer the request. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, applies that principle by retrieving relevant document chunks instead of routinely sending an entire document.

2.6 What Is an API?

An Application Programming Interface, or API, lets one program communicate with another. Here, your Python app sends a request to an AI provider and receives a model response that it can display or process.

The request uses an API key, a model name, the prompt and any applicable settings. This chapter’s example uses the OpenAI Python SDK, the OpenAI client and the Responses API. It reads generated text through response.output_text. Keep those provider-specific details inside the client so the rest of your application can use a smaller interface.

2.7 Why Use a Reusable Client?

The later projects include a command-line assistant, RAG applications, tools, memory, workflows, research, guardrails, evaluation and a deployed capstone. Each will need a way to obtain a model response. A shared client avoids copying the request setup into every project.

The application can call:

client.complete(system=system_prompt, user=user_prompt)

If you change a model setting, add logging or retries, or implement support for another provider, there is one defined place to work on that behaviour. The prompt for a particular task can remain with the application that uses it.

2.8 Model Selection

Models differ in availability, cost, speed and suitability for tasks such as reasoning, coding, structured output, long-context processing and tool use. For the learning projects, choose a model you can access and afford, with support in the provider’s SDK, then check its responses on your examples.

The model name is configured through .env so it can be changed without editing the application:

OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini

Treat this as the example’s configuration, not a permanent recommendation. Model names, pricing, capabilities and API behaviour can change. Check the provider’s documentation and your account’s access before running or deploying the application.

2.9 Temperature

Temperature affects the variation in generated responses. Where the model supports this setting, a lower value is commonly used when consistent wording or structure matters, while a higher value allows more variation. It does not guarantee correctness or identical output.

The example setting is:

OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

For this book’s technical exercises, around 0.2 is a starting point to test. Code explanation, RAG answers, structured output, data extraction, business workflows and evaluation-sensitive applications often need restrained variation. Brainstorming, creative writing, naming ideas and marketing drafts may benefit from exploring higher values, provided you review the results.

2.10 Cost Awareness

API charges generally depend on usage. The inputs to consider include input tokens, output tokens, model choice and the number of calls. A small assistant might use one model call, while a multi-agent workflow might use five. A RAG answer may include a long document excerpt, and a tool-using agent may call the model once to choose a tool and again to explain its result.

During development, use short examples, retrieve only the context needed and avoid calls that do not contribute to the task. Test local Python behaviour without the API and use a mock when you need a predictable response. Track calls as the application grows so you can see where usage comes from. Chapter 11 introduces a simple cost-estimation system.

2.11 Keeping Provider Details Separate

The examples use an OpenAI-style implementation, but your application can depend on your own client.complete(system, user) interface. That keeps its prompt and business logic separate from the provider’s request format.

You could later implement OpenAIClient, AnthropicClient, LocalModelClient or MockClient behind the same basic interface. Each implementation would handle the details of its provider while giving the calling code a familiar method.

2.12 Project: Reusable Python LLM Client

What the Client Does

The project creates a Python class that reads configuration, validates prompts and checks for an API key only when a live request is needed. It sends instructions and user input separately, returns completed text and reports failures explicitly. The fixed-response mock and controlled-transport tests run without a real key or a live API.

Where You Will Use It

You can reuse this client when learning a new application pattern, building a portfolio project or developing tools for a client. It gives you a place to maintain common behaviour while each application keeps its own task-specific code.

Project Files

Create this structure:

chapter_02_llm_client/
    .env.example
    .gitignore
    PROVIDER_NOTES.md
    README.md
    demo.py
    examples/config_excerpt.py
    examples/interface_excerpt.py
    examples/live_usage.py
    examples/provider_sketches.py
    llm_client.py
    mock_demo.py
    requirements.txt
    safe_client.py
    test_llm_client.py
    verification/compileall.txt
    verification/pytest.txt

2.13 Setup

Step 1: Create the Folder

mkdir chapter_02_llm_client
cd chapter_02_llm_client

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

python -m venv .venv

Activate the environment using the command for your shell. On macOS or Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Step 3: Create requirements.txt

Create requirements.txt with these versions, used for this edition’s offline tests:

openai==3.13.0
python-dotenv==1.2.3
pytest==9.1.1
httpx2==2.12.0

Install the dependencies in the active virtual environment:

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Create .env.example

OPENAI_API_KEY=
OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini
OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

Copy the example to .env. On macOS or Linux:

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Edit .env and add your API key. Keep the file private, and use the placeholder values in .env.example when sharing the project’s setup.

"""Chapter 2: A reusable LLM client with a separately testable API boundary."""

import math
import os
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Protocol

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from openai import APIError, OpenAI

load_dotenv(Path(__file__).with_name(".env"))


def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float:
    """Return a finite environment float, or the default for invalid input."""
    try:
        value = float(os.getenv(name, str(default)))
    except ValueError:
        return default
    return value if math.isfinite(value) else default


@dataclass
class LLMConfig:
    """Settings for this example; other models may support different options."""

    model: str = field(
        default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini")
    )
    temperature: float = field(
        default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2)
    )

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not isinstance(self.model, str) or not self.model.strip():
            raise ValueError("Model name cannot be empty.")
        if (
            isinstance(self.temperature, bool)
            or not isinstance(self.temperature, (int, float))
            or not math.isfinite(self.temperature)
            or not 0 <= self.temperature <= 2
        ):
            raise ValueError("Temperature must be a finite number from 0 to 2.")


class LLMProvider(Protocol):
    """The small interface applications depend on, independent of provider."""

    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        """Return model-generated text."""
        ...


def _validate_prompts(system: str, user: str) -> None:
    if not isinstance(system, str) or not system.strip():
        raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty and must be text.")
    if not isinstance(user, str) or not user.strip():
        raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty and must be text.")


class LLMClient:
    """Create a live SDK client only when a valid request actually needs it.

    Pass a client using a controlled transport for offline integration tests.
    A supplied client remains the caller's responsibility to close.
    """

    def __init__(
        self, config: LLMConfig | None = None, *, client: OpenAI | None = None
    ) -> None:
        self.config = config or LLMConfig()
        self.client = client
        self._owns_client = client is None

    def build_input(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        """Validate prompts and return their labelled text for inspection.

        This compatibility helper does not establish API roles. complete()
        sends the two strings using separate instructions and input fields.
        """
        _validate_prompts(system, user)
        return f"System instruction:\n{system.strip()}\n\nUser request:\n{user.strip()}"

    def _get_client(self) -> OpenAI:
        if self.client is None:
            api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY", "").strip()
            if not api_key or api_key in {"replace_with_your_api_key", "your_api_key"}:
                raise ValueError("OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file.")
            self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key, timeout=30.0, max_retries=0)
        return self.client

    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        """Return completed text or raise a clear setup/provider error.

        No automatic retries are made by this example. Do not treat an error
        message as model output or silently substitute a mock response.
        """
        self.build_input(system=system, user=user)
        try:
            response = self._get_client().responses.create(
                model=self.config.model,
                instructions=system.strip(),
                input=user.strip(),
                temperature=self.config.temperature,
            )
        except APIError as error:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "The model request failed. Check the network, model access "
                "and API account configuration."
            ) from error
        if response.status != "completed":
            raise RuntimeError("The model did not complete the response.")
        if not response.output_text.strip():
            raise RuntimeError("The model returned no text output.")
        return response.output_text

    def close(self) -> None:
        """Release the SDK client owned by this wrapper; permit later reuse."""
        if self._owns_client and self.client is not None:
            self.client.close()
            self.client = None


class MockLLMClient:
    """Return a fixed reply and record calls without a network or API key."""

    def __init__(self, response_text: str = "Mock response") -> None:
        self.response_text = response_text
        self.calls: list[dict[str, str]] = []

    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        _validate_prompts(system, user)
        self.calls.append({"system": system, "user": user})
        return self.response_text

2.16 File: demo.py

"""Print one tutoring response; the default route requires a real API key."""

from llm_client import LLMClient, LLMProvider

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a helpful Python tutor.
Explain concepts clearly for beginner-to-intermediate learners.
Be concise and practical.
Do not invent facts.
"""


def main(client: LLMProvider | None = None) -> int:
    """Allow an injected provider when testing the CLI without a live model."""
    provider = None
    try:
        provider = client if client is not None else LLMClient()
        response = provider.complete(
            system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
            user="Explain Python dictionaries in one paragraph with a simple example.",
        )
    except ValueError:
        print("Setup error: OPENAI_API_KEY is missing or the model configuration is invalid.")
        return 1
    except RuntimeError:
        print("API error: The model request failed or returned no complete text response.")
        return 1
    finally:
        if client is None and provider is not None:
            provider.close()
    print(response)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

"""Original local checks plus real SDK tests using a controlled HTTP transport."""

import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys

import httpx2
import pytest
from openai import OpenAI

import demo
import llm_client
from llm_client import LLMClient, LLMConfig, MockLLMClient, get_env_float


def test_get_env_float_returns_default_when_missing(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.delenv("TEST_FLOAT", raising=False)
    assert get_env_float("TEST_FLOAT", 0.2) == 0.2


def test_get_env_float_returns_default_when_invalid(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("TEST_FLOAT", "not-a-number")
    assert get_env_float("TEST_FLOAT", 0.2) == 0.2


def test_get_env_float_reads_valid_value(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("TEST_FLOAT", "0.7")
    assert get_env_float("TEST_FLOAT", 0.2) == 0.7


def test_llm_config_can_be_created():
    config = LLMConfig(model="test-model", temperature=0.1)
    assert config.model == "test-model"
    assert config.temperature == 0.1


def test_mock_client_returns_response():
    client = MockLLMClient(response_text="Hello from mock")
    assert client.complete(system="You are helpful.", user="Say hello.") == "Hello from mock"


def test_mock_client_records_calls():
    client = MockLLMClient(response_text="Mock response")
    client.complete(system="System prompt", user="User prompt")
    assert client.calls == [{"system": "System prompt", "user": "User prompt"}]


def test_mock_client_rejects_empty_system():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        MockLLMClient().complete(system=" ", user="Hello")


def test_mock_client_rejects_empty_user():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        MockLLMClient().complete(system="You are helpful.", user=" ")


@pytest.mark.parametrize("raw", ["nan", "inf", "-inf"])
def test_nonfinite_environment_float_falls_back(monkeypatch, raw):
    monkeypatch.setenv("TEST_FLOAT", raw)
    assert get_env_float("TEST_FLOAT", 0.2) == 0.2


@pytest.mark.parametrize("value", [-1, 3, float("nan"), True])
def test_invalid_temperature_is_rejected(value):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Temperature"):
        LLMConfig(temperature=value)


def test_empty_model_is_rejected():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Model name"):
        LLMConfig(model=" ")


def test_live_client_can_be_created_and_inspected_without_credentials(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.delenv("OPENAI_API_KEY", raising=False)
    monkeypatch.setattr(llm_client, "OpenAI", lambda **_: pytest.fail("SDK constructed"))
    client = LLMClient()
    assert client.client is None
    assert client.build_input(" Tutor ", " Explain lists ") == (
        "System instruction:\nTutor\n\nUser request:\nExplain lists"
    )
    client.close()
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="OPENAI_API_KEY is missing"):
        client.complete("Tutor", "Explain lists")


@pytest.mark.parametrize("system,user", [(" ", "Hi"), ("Tutor", " "), (None, "Hi"), ("Tutor", 1)])
def test_invalid_input_is_rejected_before_client_creation(monkeypatch, system, user):
    monkeypatch.setattr(llm_client, "OpenAI", lambda **_: pytest.fail("SDK constructed"))
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        LLMClient().complete(system, user)


def response_payload(text="Controlled reply", status="completed"):
    return {
        "id": "resp_offline", "object": "response", "created_at": 0,
        "status": status, "model": "gpt-4.1-mini",
        "output": [{
            "type": "message", "id": "msg_offline", "status": "completed",
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": [{"type": "output_text", "text": text, "annotations": []}],
        }],
        "parallel_tool_calls": True, "tool_choice": "auto", "tools": [],
    }


def offline_client(handler):
    return OpenAI(
        api_key="offline-test-key", max_retries=0,
        http_client=httpx2.Client(
            transport=httpx2.MockTransport(handler), trust_env=False
        ),
    )


def test_real_sdk_request_has_distinct_instructions_and_user_input(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.delenv("OPENAI_API_KEY", raising=False)
    requests = []
    def handler(request):
        requests.append(request)
        return httpx2.Response(200, json=response_payload())
    with offline_client(handler) as sdk:
        client = LLMClient(LLMConfig(model="gpt-4.1-mini", temperature=0.1), client=sdk)
        assert client.complete(" Tutor ", " What is a list? ") == "Controlled reply"
        client.close()
        assert not sdk.is_closed(), "Caller owns injected SDK client"
    assert len(requests) == 1
    assert requests[0].url.path == "/v1/responses"
    data = json.loads(requests[0].content)
    assert data["instructions"] == "Tutor"
    assert data["input"] == "What is a list?"
    assert data["model"] == "gpt-4.1-mini"
    assert data["temperature"] == 0.1


def test_sdk_is_constructed_lazily_reused_and_closed(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("OPENAI_API_KEY", "offline-test-key")
    calls = []
    sdk = offline_client(lambda _: httpx2.Response(200, json=response_payload()))
    def create(**kwargs):
        calls.append(kwargs)
        return sdk
    monkeypatch.setattr(llm_client, "OpenAI", create)
    client = LLMClient()
    assert calls == []
    assert client.complete("Tutor", "A") == "Controlled reply"
    assert client.complete("Tutor", "B") == "Controlled reply"
    assert len(calls) == 1
    assert calls[0]["max_retries"] == 0
    client.close()
    assert sdk.is_closed()
    assert client.client is None


@pytest.mark.parametrize("status,text,message", [
    ("incomplete", "partial", "did not complete"),
    ("completed", "", "no text"),
])
def test_incomplete_and_empty_provider_output_rejected(status, text, message):
    with offline_client(lambda _: httpx2.Response(
        200, json=response_payload(text=text, status=status)
    )) as sdk:
        with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match=message):
            LLMClient(client=sdk).complete("Tutor", "A")


def test_provider_error_is_explicit_and_does_not_echo_response_body():
    with offline_client(lambda _: httpx2.Response(429, json={
        "error": {"message": "private-account-detail", "type": "rate_limit_error"}
    })) as sdk:
        with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="model request failed") as failure:
            LLMClient(client=sdk).complete("Tutor", "A")
    assert "private-account-detail" not in str(failure.value)


def test_transport_failure_is_explicit():
    def handler(request):
        raise httpx2.ConnectError("offline", request=request)
    with offline_client(handler) as sdk:
        with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="model request failed"):
            LLMClient(client=sdk).complete("Tutor", "A")


def test_mock_calls_are_not_shared_between_instances():
    first, second = MockLLMClient(), MockLLMClient()
    first.complete("Tutor", "A")
    assert second.calls == []


def test_demo_uses_injected_provider(capsys):
    provider = MockLLMClient("Controlled demo reply")
    assert demo.main(provider) == 0
    assert capsys.readouterr().out == "Controlled demo reply\n"
    assert provider.calls[0]["user"] == (
        "Explain Python dictionaries in one paragraph with a simple example."
    )


def test_demo_handles_missing_key_without_traceback(monkeypatch, capsys):
    monkeypatch.delenv("OPENAI_API_KEY", raising=False)
    assert demo.main() == 1
    assert "Setup error:" in capsys.readouterr().out


def test_demo_handles_provider_failure_without_sensitive_details(capsys):
    class FailedProvider:
        def complete(self, system, user):
            raise RuntimeError("private-account-detail")
    assert demo.main(FailedProvider()) == 1
    output = capsys.readouterr().out
    assert "API error:" in output
    assert "private-account-detail" not in output


def test_demo_handles_invalid_configuration(monkeypatch, capsys):
    monkeypatch.setenv("OPENAI_MODEL", " ")
    assert demo.main() == 1
    assert "Setup error:" in capsys.readouterr().out


def test_actual_entrypoint_missing_key_is_controlled():
    environment = dict(os.environ)
    environment["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = ""
    result = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "demo.py"], capture_output=True, text=True,
        env=environment, timeout=10, check=False,
    )
    assert result.returncode == 1
    assert "Setup error:" in result.stdout
    assert "Traceback" not in result.stderr


def test_actual_mock_demo_entrypoint_is_offline():
    environment = dict(os.environ)
    environment["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = ""
    result = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "mock_demo.py"], capture_output=True, text=True,
        env=environment, timeout=10, check=True,
    )
    assert "Offline mock example" in result.stdout
    assert "dictionary stores key-value pairs" in result.stdout


def test_optional_safe_wrapper_preserves_successful_text():
    from safe_client import SafeLLMClient
    with offline_client(lambda _: httpx2.Response(200, json=response_payload())) as sdk:
        assert SafeLLMClient(client=sdk).complete_safe("Tutor", "A") == "Controlled reply"


def test_optional_safe_wrapper_does_not_expose_provider_error_body():
    from safe_client import SafeLLMClient
    with offline_client(lambda _: httpx2.Response(429, json={
        "error": {"message": "private-account-detail", "type": "rate_limit_error"}
    })) as sdk:
        result = SafeLLMClient(client=sdk).complete_safe("Tutor", "A")
    assert result.startswith("LLM error:")
    assert "private-account-detail" not in result

2.18 File: README.md

# Reusable Python LLM Client

A reusable client with the chapter's `complete(system, user)` interface. Python 3.10 or newer is required; the packaged verification used Python 3.12.

## Features

- Environment-based model and temperature configuration.
- API-key lookup and SDK construction deferred until a valid request needs them.
- Separate API `instructions` and `input` fields for standing instructions and the changing user request.
- An inspectable `build_input()` helper, retained for teaching and compatibility.
- An injected-client option and a fixed-response `MockLLMClient` for local tests.
- Explicit setup, transport/provider and empty/incomplete-response errors.

## Setup

From this project folder on macOS or Linux:

```sh
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env
```

On Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
Copy-Item .env.example .env
```

## Interface and ownership

`LLMClient(config=None, *, client=None)` accepts a real SDK client with an offline transport. The caller owns an injected client. `close()` closes only SDK clients created by the wrapper. `build_input()` produces labelled text for inspection, while `complete()` sends the actual prompts as separate API fields. This is a deliberate correction to the flattened source's combined input string.

`MockLLMClient` validates prompts, returns a fixed reply and records calls per instance. It measures caller behaviour, not live generation. `mock_demo.py` is explicitly labelled as an offline mock example. `PROVIDER_NOTES.md` describes how to implement another provider without pretending the book includes a complete integration for it.

`safe_client.py` includes a completed version of the optional public error-wrapper exercise, with tests for successful output and non-disclosure of provider error bodies. Optional logging and character-limit exercises remain exercises. Avoid logging credentials or full sensitive prompts. A public error wrapper should return a controlled message rather than the raw exception body.

2.19 How the Code Works

The client is organised around configuration, an interface and two implementations of that interface.

Part 1: Configuration

LLMConfig holds the settings used by the live client:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class LLMConfig:
    model: str
    temperature: float

The full class loads default values from OPENAI_MODEL and OPENAI_TEMPERATURE. You can adjust those environment variables without changing the calling code.

Part 2: Provider Interface

The LLMProvider protocol describes the method the application expects:

from typing import Protocol


class LLMProvider(Protocol):
    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        ...

A different provider class can implement the same method. The application can then ask it to complete a request without having to know how that provider sends it.

Part 3: Live Client

LLMClient can be constructed without an API key. Its first valid live request obtains the key and constructs the SDK client; later calls reuse that client. It returns completed, nonempty text or raises an explicit error. Call close() when finished; an SDK client supplied by the caller remains the caller’s responsibility.

Part 4: Mock Client

MockLLMClient returns a fixed response and records the calls it receives. This lets tests check what the application sent and how it handled the reply without paying for a model call or waiting for the network. Those tests assess the application logic; they do not measure a live model’s answer quality.

2.24 Designing for Another Provider

The application expects an object with complete(system, user). That object might call OpenAI, Anthropic, a local model or a future provider, or it might return a mock response. The following sketches show possible implementations of the shared interface; they are not complete provider integrations.

class AnthropicClient:
    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError("Implement the provider integration first.")

A local implementation could follow the same pattern:

class LocalModelClient:
    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError("Implement the local model integration first.")

A mock can supply a fixed reply:

class MockLLMClient:
    def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        return "Mock response"

Keeping this boundary small makes it easier to adapt the client without spreading provider-specific choices through your application.

2.25 Common API Errors

Error 1: Missing API Key

If OPENAI_API_KEY is not set, create or check .env and add the key there. Confirm that the application loads the file.

Error 2: Wrong Model Name

The configured model may be misspelled or unavailable to your account. Compare it with the provider’s model list and your available access.

Error 3: Package Not Installed

If openai or python-dotenv is missing, install the requirements in the environment used to run the application:

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Error 4: Running from the Wrong Folder

If the project’s configuration is not being found, return to its folder and run the demo there:

cd chapter_02_llm_client
python demo.py

Error 5: Expecting Identical Wording

Model responses can vary even at a low temperature. For live-output tests, check the required meaning and structure where appropriate. Exact-string assertions are better suited to behaviour you control, such as a fixed mock response.

2.26 Developing Without Unnecessary API Calls

Use the following sequence to separate local problems from problems with the live call:

  1. Write the prompt builder functions.
  2. Test the strings those functions produce without calling the model.
  3. Use a mock client to test application logic and response handling.
  4. Run a live API test after the local flow works.
  5. Capture actual outputs when preparing examples that you intend to report as observed results.

This keeps routine debugging from consuming API credits. If an application fails before sending a valid prompt, you can investigate its Python logic without relying on another model response.

2.27 Using the Client Across an Application

A freelance automation application might contain analyze_client_message(), draft_proposal(), draft_followup_email() and review_output(). Each has a different purpose, but each can use the same client to send its prompt.

A document assistant might use answer_question_from_context(), summarize_document() and generate_followup_questions(). A multi-agent workflow might use planner_agent(), researcher_agent(), writer_agent() and reviewer_agent(). Sharing the client in these designs gives you one place to maintain request handling while keeping the task functions distinct.

2.29 Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Copying API Calls Everywhere

Duplicated request code means duplicated maintenance. Keep the shared behaviour in the client and the task-specific prompts with their application functions.

Mistake 2: Hardcoding Secrets

Keep real API keys out of Python files and shared examples. Load them from the environment.

Mistake 3: Mixing Stable Instructions with Every New Request

Keep the assistant’s standing instructions separate from the text that changes for each task. This makes both easier to inspect and revise.

Mistake 4: Testing Everything Through the Live API

Use a mock for normal application logic, then test the live integration separately. A mock’s predictable reply helps isolate failures in your code.

Mistake 5: Ignoring Call Volume

Each model call may incur a charge. Check whether the call is needed and account for repeated calls within a workflow.

Mistake 6: Spreading Provider Details Through the App

Place provider-specific request and response handling behind your own interface so you can change it without editing every caller.

Mistake 7: Assuming the API Will Stay the Same

Check the provider’s documentation before deployment and keep the integration in one place. The model setting and SDK behaviour used by an example may need review later.

2.30 Best Practices

Use .env for local secrets and keep it out of version control. Keep model names configurable, validate empty inputs and keep the request interface in one client. Store stable assistant instructions separately from the changing user request.

Use mocks for local tests, choose supported settings appropriate to the task and review the resulting output. Track calls as the application grows, and document the environment, setup commands and live-call requirements so another developer can reproduce your checks.

Challenge 3: Add a complete_safe() Method

The companion includes safe_client.py, a completed version of this exercise. Its subclass adds complete_safe(), returns successful model text unchanged and turns expected setup/provider errors into a controlled public message. Do not include the raw exception body in a user-facing response:

from llm_client import LLMClient


class SafeLLMClient(LLMClient):
    def complete_safe(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
        try:
            return self.complete(system, user)
        except (ValueError, RuntimeError):
            return "LLM error: The request could not be completed. Check the configuration and try again."

2.32 Chapter Summary

The terminology in this chapter describes decisions you will make in each AI application: what instructions and context to send, which model and settings to use, and how requests contribute to cost. The reusable client gives those decisions a defined place in the code.

Through client.complete(system, user), a caller can request text without repeating the provider setup. The mock client lets you test callers with fixed responses. Chapter 3 uses this interface to build a command-line assistant with several commands.

Key Takeaways

  • A language model works within an application that handles input, context, tools and output.
  • Prompts should specify the task, audience and any response structure you need.
  • Separate standing instructions from the current request in your application design.
  • Consider token usage, context, model choice and call volume when managing cost and response time.
  • Use a reusable client to contain provider-specific request handling.
  • Use a mock to test local behaviour, and evaluate live responses separately.
  • Check model access and current API requirements before running or deploying the examples.
